subject: health
unitTitle: Food, Water, and Moving My Body
title: Explicit model: food allergies and safe sharing
essentialQuestion: How do food, water, and movement give my body energy for the things I want to do?
materials: paper and pencil or an accessible response tool
the fictional lesson cards included in this task
keyPoints: A food allergy is the body reacting to a food as if it were dangerous, and it can be serious very fast.
Common ones include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and sesame.
Never share or swap food with someone who has an allergy unless a trusted adult has checked it.
Signs to get an adult for immediately: swelling of the face or lips, a rash, trouble breathing, or vomiting after eating.
Wash hands after eating an allergen so it is not left on shared surfaces.
privacySafeScenario: All required evidence uses fictional or public situations. The learner never has to disclose personal health, body, treatment, feelings, family, sexual, or substance-use information.
studentTask: Write two facts. Use the lesson idea about food allergies and safe sharing. Choose one safe next step. Name an adult or help source.
knowledgeCheck: Name the fact. Fix the wrong claim. Choose a safe action. Name who can help.
completionCriteria: I explain food allergies and safe sharing.
I choose a safe action and give a reason.
I name the right kind of help.
adaptationChoices: Show one short direction at a time. Allow reading aloud, word cards, typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking. Help may repeat a direction but may not choose the fact, action, reason, or help source.
extensionChallenge: Create a new fictional or public case about food allergies and safe sharing. Include enough facts, choices or constraints, and support authority for another learner to reason safely. Add an accurate explanation of acceptable variation; use no real person's private information.
accessibilitySupports: Show one action at a time.
Offer a vocabulary card and extra time.
Accept typing, writing, drawing with labels, signing, selecting, or speaking for equal credit.
trustedAdultNote: If a real situation feels unsafe or raises a health concern, pause the lesson and tell a parent, guardian, teacher, school staff member, or another trusted adult. A qualified health professional gives medical advice. In an emergency, get an adult and use the local emergency service.

optionalReflection.prompt: Optional and private: Make up one example that helps you remember food allergies and safe sharing. Keep it for yourself. You do not need to show it or prove that you completed it.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, body-fat percentage, body comparison, or appearance scoring.
This task never requires calorie counting, dieting, or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires sharing medical history, a diagnosis, treatment, medication, feelings, family conflict, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.
This task never requires advice about an individual learner's treatment, medication, food, supplement, or exercise plan.

Michigan Health Practice 5: Self-Management and Goal Setting
Michigan Health Topic (Grades 3-5): Balanced Eating and Physical Activity

modelExample.heading: Watch the reasoning: food allergies and safe sharing
modelExample.situation: A fictional Northside class reads a display about food allergies and safe sharing. The display states: A food allergy is the body reacting to a food as if it were dangerous, and it can be serious very fast. One visitor says that this single fact proves what kind of person someone is. The class must explain the concept and correct the overclaim.
relevantFacts: A food allergy is the body reacting to a food as if it were dangerous, and it can be serious very fast.
Common ones include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and sesame.
modelExample.assumptionOrDistraction: A popular or confident statement about food allergies and safe sharing is not automatically accurate and cannot establish a person's health, motives, or character.
possibleActions: Explain the concept with the stated fact and correct the person label.
Repeat the topic word without defining it.
Treat one detail as proof of a diagnosis or a person's value.
modelExample.successCheck: The model uses the lesson fact, explains the connection, stays within the learner role, and names responsible help when it is needed.
workedReasoning: Name the lesson concept and explain it with the reference-card fact.
Separate what the concept means from a label or unsupported conclusion about a person.
Apply the concept to one safe action and name the right help source if the situation needs one.

guidedReasoning.heading: Try a different case with support
guidedReasoning.situation: A fictional Riverside youth group must explain or act on food allergies and safe sharing. The group has this reliable lesson information: Common ones include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and sesame. It has not been given any person's private health information.
availableChoices: Use the stated facts and compare safe options.
Pause and contact the responsible help source.
turnOne: Name an adult who can help.
guidedReasoning.cue: Look for the situation, safe choices, relevant information, and who can help.
feedbackMoves: If a response adds a guess, replace it with a fact from the case or lesson.
If food allergies and safe sharing is named without explanation, link one fact to the concept or process.
If a choice is reasonable but the reason is missing, add the fact that supports it.
If a response seeks disclosure, diagnoses, shames, or exceeds the learner role, switch to the fictional facts and the approved help route.
Accept an equivalent typed, handwritten, drawn-and-labeled, signed, selected, or spoken response when it shows the same reasoning.
guidedReasoning.turnTwo: Fix one sentence. Use a fact and a safe next step.
guidedReasoning.releaseCondition: Continue when the response uses a stated fact, applies food allergies and safe sharing, and gives a safe next step without private disclosure or a person label.

freshMasteryCheck.heading: Check the idea in a new place
freshMasteryCheck.situation: A fictional Lakeside school committee reviews food allergies and safe sharing. The committee knows: Never share or swap food with someone who has an allergy unless a trusted adult has checked it. It must correct one unsupported claim and choose a safe next step.

remediation.heading: Try a different model
remediation.trigger: Use this route after an observable gap in a fact, vocabulary meaning, reasoning step, process order, or help route for food allergies and safe sharing.
remediation.prerequisite: First restate this approved fact in your own words: A food allergy is the body reacting to a food as if it were dangerous, and it can be serious very fast.
remediation.alternateExplanation: Use a four-box decision map: SITUATION, SAFE CHOICES, RELEVANT INFORMATION, and HELP. Fill each box with case facts before writing a conclusion.
contrast: Sufficient: uses a stated fact about food allergies and safe sharing, explains the connection, and stays within the learner role.
Needs revision: repeats a topic word, adds a guess, or gives an action with no factual reason or responsible help source.
remediation.guidedCorrection: Cross out the guess. Circle the fact. Add one safe action.

freshRetry.situation: A fictional Oak Street library receives a new question about food allergies and safe sharing. Staff provide this approved fact: Common ones include peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, fish, shellfish, and sesame. The learner must respond without using the Northside, Riverside, Maple, or Lakeside conclusions.

remediation.exitCriterion: Return to the independent route when the learner accurately uses a fact, applies food allergies and safe sharing, explains a safe response, and identifies support without answer-bearing help.
remediation.nextRoute: If the same gap remains, return to the named prerequisite with an adult instructor; do not replace the task with private reflection.

laterTransfer.timing: Use in a later lesson or a separate session.

laterTransfer.masteryBoundary: The current independent response is one evidence occasion. Mastery requires accurate independent evidence now and accurate later retrieval or transfer.
